title: HF vs. VHF vs. UHF
idea: Each range is ten times the one below it. HF bounces off the ionosphere; VHF and UHF mostly stop near the horizon.

rows: Reflected by the ionosphere: long distance is far more common
Line of sight, plus a little: the atmosphere bends it slightly
Usually not propagated by the ionosphere, so it stops near the horizon

config.heading: Three ranges, each ten times the last
config.lead: Tap a range to see how it travels. The scale grows by ten at each step.

bands.name: HF, VHF and UHF
bands.text: Each range runs from a number to ten times that number: 3 to 30, 30 to 300, 300 to 3000 MHz.

segs.label: HF
segs.text: 3 to 30 MHz. The ionosphere can reflect HF, so long-distance contacts are far more common here than on VHF and up.

segs.label: VHF
segs.text: 30 to 300 MHz. The radio horizon is a bit farther than the visual horizon, because the atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly.

segs.label: UHF
segs.text: 300 to 3000 MHz. UHF signals are usually not propagated by the ionosphere, so simplex UHF is rarely heard beyond the radio horizon.

compare.how: Reflects HF. That's the long-distance layer.
A little past the visual horizon: the atmosphere bends VHF and UHF slightly.

traps.why: Watch the units. HF is 3 to 30 MHz. 300 to 3000 kHz is a lower range.
Right digits, wrong unit. VHF is 30 to 300 MHz.
Right digits, wrong unit. UHF is 300 to 3000 MHz.
The troposphere is where ducting happens. HF is reflected by the ionosphere.

traps.wrong: FCC regulations prohibit them from going more than 50 miles
traps.why: No such rule. UHF just isn't usually propagated by the ionosphere.

traps.wrong: Radio signals move somewhat faster than the speed of light
traps.why: Nothing does. The atmosphere bends radio waves slightly, carrying them past the visual horizon.
HF has longer waves, so HF antennas are bigger. The answer is long-distance ionospheric propagation.
